newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia economy stagnant despite bright spots.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia economy stagnant despite bright spots.

text.p: The Russian economy will achieve zero growth in 1997, a deputy minister said on Tuesday after official figures showed the economy unchanged over the first four months despite some progress in payment of wage arrears.

Russian gross domestic product (GDP) -- the widest measure of economic output -- was steady over the first four months of 1997 versus the same period a year ago. April GDP fell one percent on last year.
"Towards the end of 1997, (GDP) will be at the same level as 1996 -- that is, we will achieve zero growth," First Deputy Economy Minister Ivan Matyorov told the State Duma lower house of parliament.
Russian officials forecast two percent 1997 growth early in the year but recently lowered their forecasts because of poor official indicators and budget problems.
The situation for Russian workers improved slightly as the state paid wage arrears, though industry fell further behind.
Total back wages owed at the end of April amounted to 52.62 trillion roubles ($9 billion) against 52.67 trillion in late March. The state owed 10.76 trillion compared to 11.31 trillion in March.
Unemployment was steady in April on March at 6.99 million, representing just under 10 percent of the work force.

But Russian industry, which saw April output edge up 0.5 percent year-on-year, is falling further and deeper into a nonpayment of debt crisis, First Deputy Finance Minister Vladimir Panskov was quoted by Prime-Tass news agency as saying.
Panskov told a tax conference nonpayments between industrial enterprises had reached 1,000 trillion roubles ($174 billion). GDP over the first four months was only 810 trillion roubles.

Matyorov said a suggestion by some Duma members to print money to cover an enormous budget deficit deterred investors from putting their money into Russia. The government has proposed slicing 1997 spending by around one fifth to deal with the gap.

"Even talk about doubling the monetary base and the possibility of increasing yields on government securities by itself influences investors and shoots down the possibility of movement and the return of (flight) capital," Matyorov said.
Russians are estimated to hold some $20 billion in savings in dollars tucked under their mattresses where it cannot be invested in the economy.
Billions more in export profits are never repatriated by companies eager to avoid taxes or preferring to invest abroad, economists say.
Matyorov said Russian non-ferrous metals exports were crucial to maintaining even zero growth as some areas of the economy contracted.

Russia's trade surplus, powered by exports of raw materials such as oil and non-ferrous metals, widened to $6.74 billion in the first quarter from $5.45 billion in the first three months of last year.
Russia is the world's largest exporter of primary aluminium, one of the top two producers of nickel, and the third largest producer of oil, all of which saw output rises.
Russian crude production over the first four months edged up to 97.1 million tonnes (nearly six million barrels per day), almost 10 percent of world oil demand.
Nickel production rose one percent in April over March and aluminium output rose two percent.
